profiled_workloads.selection_reason: Smallest workload (fp16, 1024 elems) and near-lowest speedup (0.540): tests whether the ~19us eval latency is launch-bound rather than device-bound
Medium regime (fp16, 1048576 elems): locates the host/device crossover between 1K and 16.7M elements
Lowest speedup in the whole set (0.441) and the 4096x4096 fp16 device-bound regime
bf16 control on the identical 4096x4096 shape: the bf16 reference is 25.4us versus 15.9us for fp16, which discriminates a conversion-cost hypothesis from a pure bandwidth limit
Highest eval latency (0.0390ms) and highest speedup (0.857): the fp32 4096x4096 regime, where the candidate is closest to reference

findings.label: Per-call launch cost dominates all nine workloads with numel <= 1M; the device kernel occupies only 5-19% of the period

evidence.metric: avg kernel duration _log10_nomask (1024 fp16, 100 invocations, min 1.08 / max 3.70)
mean kernel start-to-start interval (tasks 2..111, 109 intervals, span 2433.27us)
mean kernel start-to-start interval (tasks 2..111, 109 intervals, span 2668.63us)

findings.inference: For fp16/1024 the profiled device stream shows a mean 22.3us start-to-start period around a 1.2-1.5us kernel, i.e. about 94% of the period the stream is idle waiting for the next submission; eval latency for the same workload is 19.44us (reference 10.50us). At 1M elements the kernel grows to 4.6us but the period grows to 24.5us, so the host still sets the pace. The profiled periods exceed eval latency by 2-5us, which is consistent with msprof instrumentation overhead, so these intervals are an upper bound on the host cost, not a direct measurement of it. Because eval latency (~18-20us) minus kernel time (1.5-4.6us) leaves ~15-18us unaccounted, at least 75% of the eval latency on these nine workloads is outside kernel execution. The device artifacts cannot separate a Python-level wrapper from the pybind/CANN launch from the harness dispatch; that split is unresolved and is the object of the next experiment.

findings.label: The three 4096x4096 workloads are AIV-bound at ~96% with strictly additive (non-overlapped) pipelines

evidence.metric: mean kernel start-to-start interval equals kernel duration for fp16 4096x4096 (tasks 3..11: 290.045us / 8)

findings.inference: In all three large cases the AIV pipeline times sum to ~100% of aiv_time (fp16 35.07/34.83, bf16 37.15/36.91, fp32 37.86/37.64), and aiv_time is 96% of kernel duration, while per-invocation values are constant to within 1.5% across 100 calls. Additive pipeline occupancy of ~100% means the block load (MTE2), vector compute, and store (MTE3) of the single 32768-element tile are effectively serialized rather than overlapped; the kernel is a single load/compute/store with 512 programs and no cross-tile pipelining. Their start-to-start interval equals kernel duration (36.26us vs 36.23us), so these three workloads are already device-bound and no further host reduction can help them.

findings.label: fp16/bf16 4096x4096 pay ~7-9us of extra vector time for the fp32 detour at identical element and program count

evidence.metric: vec_time 20.169us (ratio 0.579) for fp16, 16777216 elems, 512 programs, BLOCK 32768
vec_time 12.959us (ratio 0.344) for fp32, same 16777216 elems and same 512 programs
mte2/mte3 are byte-proportional (fp16 5.660/6.267 vs fp32 10.157/11.990), confirming identical tile/program structure

findings.inference: Element count, program count (Block Num 512) and tile are identical across the fp16 and fp32 runs, and the transfer times scale exactly with bytes, so the +7.2us of vector time in fp16 (and +9.3us in bf16) is attributable to the two dtype conversions around the fp32 log (x.to(float32) and the narrowing store) rather than to more log evaluations or a different tiling. The reference behaves the same way in the opposite direction: its fp16 4096x4096 latency is 15.89us while its bf16 latency is 25.37us, which suggests the reference performs log natively in fp16 but must upcast for bf16. Instruction-level confirmation was not obtained: the instruction collection for this kernel failed with the simulator deadline expiring, so the conversion attribution rests on the pipeline-counter comparison only.

findings.label: A vendor aclnn elementwise kernel overlaps MTE2/MTE3 on the same 4096x4096 fp16 shape, proving overlap is reachable on this device

evidence.metric: aclnnAdds_AddAiCore_Add on 4096x4096 fp16: duration 20.941us, aiv 17.883, mte2 10.953 (0.612), mte3 11.903 (0.666), vec 2.423 (0.135) -> ratios sum 1.50
aclnnAbs_AbsAiCore_Abs on 4096x4096 fp16: duration 32.080us, aiv 28.493, mte2 21.792 (0.765), mte3 15.665 (0.550)

findings.inference: On the same device and the same 4096x4096 fp16 shape, the vendor Adds kernel shows pipeline ratios summing to 1.50 (mte2 10.95 + mte3 11.90 exceed aiv_time 17.88), i.e. its transfers genuinely overlap each other and its compute, whereas the candidate's ratios sum to ~1.00. The Adds kernel moves more bytes than the in-place log10 (two reads plus a write versus one read plus one write) yet completes in 20.9us against the candidate's 36.2us, so a ~1.7x overlap gain on the same shape is demonstrated on this hardware. This comparison is indicative, not a matched control: Adds is a pure copy-like op with 2.4us of vector work and it ran in the harness correctness path rather than the timed loop, so it cannot be used to predict the exact log10 gain.

performance_interpretation: The round-2 change worked: geo_mean rose 0.110 -> 0.602 and the 4096x4096 latencies fell 0.60ms -> 0.036-0.039ms, and the profile confirms the device side now matches the eval timing exactly on those three shapes (kernel 36.2/38.3/39.1us versus eval 36.0/38.1/39.0us). Two distinct regimes remain. (1) All nine workloads with numel <= 1M are launch-bound: the device kernel is only 1.5-4.6us while eval latency is 17.8-20.2us, and the profiled stream shows a 22-24.5us start-to-start period around that kernel. The reference reaches 10.5-12.1us end-to-end through the same harness, which proves a materially cheaper per-call path is achievable and bounds what is left on the table at roughly 0.75-1.0x for those nine. (2) The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound with serialized pipelines; the fp16 case is the weakest (0.441) because its vector time is 20.2us versus 13.0us for fp32 at the same element count, and because nothing overlaps (~7us of that is spent below fp32). Effective byte rates implied by the authoritative eval latencies are about 1.85 TB/s (fp16 large, 67MB/36.0us), 1.76 TB/s (bf16 large) and 3.44 TB/s (fp32 large), against 4.0-4.2 TB/s implied by the reference on the same shapes; these are arithmetic ratios from eval latency and total bytes, not measured bandwidth and not a roofline claim. Neither the 168MB L2 size nor these rates establish a hardware ceiling. The dominant bound for the round as a whole is launch, because it governs nine of twelve workloads and at least 75% of their latency.

next_experiment.action_description: Attack the residual per-call host cost on the cached fast path, in two steps. (a) Bounded debug probe first, to avoid spending an eval round blind: time a loop of the current cached closure, a bare pybind call with all arguments pre-bound and the stream value already resolved, a variant that passes the data pointer as an int instead of the tensor object, and an empty Python loop, all on a 1024-element fp16 tensor without per-iteration synchronisation. That isolates Python-wrapper cost, argument marshalling, and the CANN launch itself. (b) Then shrink the per-call path in main.py to a single dict lookup plus one pybind call: fold dtype, numel and the alignment bit into a two-level cache so no data_ptr()/contiguous()/dtype attribute work happens on a hit, remove the intermediate launch() Python frame by calling the bound launcher inline in run() with grid/function/metadata already bound, and keep the ordinary Triton launch as the cold/misaligned/non-contiguous fallback. Do not cache the numeric stream across calls without validating it against torch.npu.current_stream(); the no-wait raw-stream getter must stay per call or be identity-checked.
next_experiment.expected_impact: The nine sub-1M workloads sit at 17.8-20.2us against a 10.5-12.1us reference, with only 1.5-4.6us of that being kernel. Removing 3-5us of per-call host cost should move them to roughly 14-16us, i.e. speedups from 0.54-0.67 toward 0.70-0.85, which is a geo_mean of about 0.72-0.78 versus 0.602; if the probe shows the cost is dominated by argument marshalling and the int-pointer variant is materially faster, the upper end of that range is reachable. The three 4096x4096 workloads are device-bound and must come out unchanged.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Main risks: (1) dropping the per-call alignment check could send misaligned tensors down the unmasked 32768-tile path and break correctness for slices, so alignment must be decided at cache-build time with the masked/standard launch retained as fallback; (2) replacing the per-call stream getter with a cached value would break under a stream switch, so keep the current accessor or validate stream identity; (3) in-place semantics, the returned object identity and the strided path must not change. Rollback: revert to the round-2 solution (sha256 9ca39b9a86a7932e24c872f0b4f9217836fcfa6a4740502c8b70690100f4beff, geo_mean 0.602) if the probe shows the residual cost sits in pybind/CANN and cannot be removed, or if geo_mean does not improve.
success_criteria: Full evaluation PASSED with every correctness workload matched (all 24 correctness cases, required_matched_ratio 1.0), including the 0-element, 1-element, odd-length (1025) and strided cases. In-place contract preserved: the argument is the returned object, its storage is modified, and the strided path still routes through _log10_strided.
Headline geo_mean strictly above the round-2 value of 0.601965 for the same twelve timing workloads.
The nine workloads with numel <= 1M each show eval latency below 16us (from 17.8-20.2us), which requires the profiler-confirmed non-kernel share to shrink rather than the kernel time.
No regression on the three 4096x4096 workloads: log10_-timing-3, -7 and -11 stay within 3% of 36.03/38.13/38.97us, since they were measured device-bound with start-to-start equal to kernel duration.

If the probe finds the residual cost is inside pybind/CANN rather than the Python path, record that as a negative result and stop trimming the host path instead of re-evaluating further micro-optimisations.

warnings: msprof and simulator timings are diagnostic only; all speedups, latencies and reference latencies quoted come from the frozen eval comparison of round 2.

The instruction-level collection for log10_-timing-3 failed with 'profiling deadline expired during Ascend simulator kernel 0'; no instruction listing or SASS/AscendC mapping was obtained, so the dtype-conversion attribution rests on pipeline counters. The failure was not retried.
Profiled start-to-start intervals exceed the eval latencies by 2-5us, consistent with msprof instrumentation overhead; they are upper bounds on the host per-call cost, not measurements of it.

Pipeline ratios are overlapping activities of one kernel and are not additive time decomposition in general; they are read as additive here only because their sum equals aiv_time for each of the three large workloads while the vendor Adds kernel on the same shape sums to 1.50.

The reference-side device path was not captured in these profiles: only the candidate's _log10_nomask plus two unrelated harness aclnn kernels (Abs, Adds) appear, so no claim is made about which kernels or how many launches the reference executes.
No DMA/MEMCPY_ASYNC task appears for any profiled workload, so the host-side CANN runtime cost is not visible as a device task and cannot be subtracted from these traces.
open_questions: How much of the ~15-18us non-kernel time on the sub-1M workloads is the Python wrapper, how much is pybind argument marshalling, and how much is the CANN kernel launch itself? The device artifacts cannot separate them.
Does passing the device pointer as an int rather than a torch tensor to the bound launcher avoid the tensor marshalling path, and is that legal for the Ascend launcher ABI used here?

Can a pipelined loop over multiple tiles (e.g. tl.range with num_stages > 1) make MTE2 prefetch overlap vector compute in FlagTree 0.6.0 on dav-c220, which would attack the three device-bound workloads that are currently serialized?

Would computing log10 natively in fp16 remove the ~7us of conversion vector time on log10_-timing-3 while keeping the 0.015 rtol match, given the bf16 reference itself pays 25.4us and presumably cannot avoid an upcast?
Why is the bf16 4096x4096 reference 25.37us when the fp16 reference is 15.89us on the same element count, and does that difference confirm the reference performs the fp16 log without an fp32 detour?
